segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: When the original (inspired by Michael Crichton's novel of the same name) was released in 1993, the special effects Spielberg used ushered in a new era of cinema. That is because, before Jurassic Park, there was enormous distrust of digital special effects. Ron Miller, former president of Walt Disney Productions, recounts in the book "Special Effects: An Introduction to Movie Magic" that in the early 1990s, despite all the technological progress that already existed, those in charge of productions did not want to risk using these tools because of their high costs and less-than-satisfying box office returns.

segments.original: All this technological revolution made "Jurassic Park" a hit with the public. The result was more than US$1 billion in worldwide theatrical grosses, a level reached only by Titanic in 1997. That was also the year "The Lost World" was released. The film featured more numerous and more refined rendered dinosaurs than the first one, as well as effects with realistic and catastrophic potential. The growing use of computers, however, did not replace the animatronics. On the contrary, they got a technological boost. Before, they used to break down, as when the T. rex got wet in the scene where it attacks the kids' car. But the dinosaurs created by Stan Winston, the sculptor of the creature robot in Alien, became not only more modern but also water-resistant.

tracks.title: Learn more: How "The Matrix" defined the cinema of the new century (1)

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Learn more: How "The Matrix" defined the cinema of the new century.
segments.text: Learn more: How "The Matrix" defined the cinema of the new century.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: It was mid-1998 when producer Joel Silver (b. 1952) walked into a meeting room at Warner in Los Angeles and faced a group of anxious executives. In a town run on money, the suits wanted to know how the shoot was going on a science fiction film with philosophical and existentialist touches, whose concept many of them didn't understand and in which the studio had invested $60 million. That was a lot of money at stake for a film being shot in Australia, literally on the other side of the world, by two first-time directors, Lana Wachowski (b. 1965) and Lilly Wachowski (b. 1967). Silver handed each executive a 600-page bible with the entire film laid out in storyboards, and screened eight minutes of finished footage. Jaws dropped. Many swallowed hard. The project, at least from a corporate standpoint, was safe. What no one expected at that point was that The Matrix, which hit theaters on March 31, 1999, would become not only the studio's highest-grossing film to date ($460 million, a sum surpassed a few years later by Harry Potter), but also one of the most influential science fiction adventures in history.

What no one expected at that point was that The Matrix, which hit theaters on March thirty-first, nineteen ninety-nine, would become not only the studio's highest-grossing film to date (four hundred sixty million dollars, a sum surpassed a few years later by Harry Potter), but also one of the most influential science fiction adventures in history.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Although The Matrix is an original film, its influences are explicit. Like Quentin Tarantino (b. 1963), the Wachowskis borrowed sequences, narrative solutions and even sets from other films. This melting pot of ideas, however, resulted in a unique adventure that started with philosophy ("Simulacra and Simulation," by Jean Baudrillard, was required reading before the cast had even opened the script), moved through cyberpunk (William Gibson and his Neuromancer permeate the narrative from end to end), and borrowed heavily from anime (mainly Akira and Ghost in the Shell) and comics (The Invisibles, by Grant Morrison, is practically a proto-Matrix). Some of the sets were recycled from Dark City (1998), shot a year earlier in Australia, which features similar concepts of reality and illusion.

The sources were already out in the world, but no one had connected the dots the way The Matrix did. After its release, Hollywood rushed to embrace its ideas and solutions. segments.original: Of all of The Matrix's contributions to the pop culture of the new century, perhaps the greatest was "bullet time," the special effect in which time seems to freeze while the camera circles freely around the action. It wasn't created specifically for the film, but the film is where it evolved and became popular. The film's visual effects supervisor, John Gaeta, points to the anime Akira (1988), by Katsuhiro Otomo (b. 1954), and Michel Gondry's work on his music videos as the main artistic inspiration for the effect. Gaeta's innovation was to put the camera in motion around people and objects that were also moving, with revolutionary results.

tracks.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The technology goes by the name of motion capture, “capturing movement.” It works like this: the actors are filmed performing their digital characters in a large studio called “the volume.” Instead of wearing costumes or makeup, they are “adorned” with hundreds of luminous dots spread across the body and, above all, the face, to capture every bodily movement and the nuances of their expressions. Special cameras, designed to pick up the luminous dots, are placed on every side of the studio, including the ceiling. Once everything is shot, the footage of those same little dots, filmed from umpteen different angles, is sent to a supercomputer that “crunches” all the data to build a three-dimensional interpretation of where each of those luminous dots was. Every little dot on the actor corresponds to a little dot on the digital character's “puppet.” That is how, in the end, you get a 3-meter-tall blue alien with a tail.

segments.original: This was the same technique used, for example, to create Gollum in The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001). But Avatar took things to the next level. One of its distinguishing features was a real-time “pre-crunching” of the data. It made it possible to render the digital characters and environments on the monitors the production crew used to check the scenes as they were being shot. This ensured precision during filming, without the need for much touching up in post-production. But no one should be fooled into thinking the work ends there.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Motion capture alone does not work miracles, because the whole process also involves the skilled hands of digital artisans who, using the computer, create the rest of the illusion. The key to creating a realistic digital character lies in the eyes. Human eyes are very expressive, but that expression happens in a very subtle way that is hard to capture, no matter how many little luminous dots you put on the guy's face. In Avatar, you can see the care the technicians took to get around this. The Na’vi have large, expressive eyes that convey life and emotion. It is really no easy task to reproduce a creature that displays human emotions. But it is even harder to fool a human audience, used to watching humans, when filmmakers try to create digital characters who are, for all intents and purposes, people just like us.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: It may seem like a foolish effort to try to recreate a human being on a computer, since it is much easier to simply film one. Now ask whether anyone wants to be filmed falling from a height of several meters, smashing into the ground, and then being trampled by a stampede of elephants, all in the same scene, without cuts. segments.original: The Middle-earth of The Lord of the Rings was a triumph of technique, blending real elements with artificial ones to reproduce with astonishing perfection the world created by J.R.R. Tolkien. But Avatar represents an evolution, because on Pandora everything is new and artificially built. Floating mountains, gigantic trees, flying dragons, monstrous creatures, exotic plants and everything else. This all-out hodgepodge may seem forced and unconvincing on paper, but on screen, with all the technical advances, seeing is believing. By bringing all these visual effects advances together in a single film, Avatar has certainly already become a landmark in film history.
